blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high-surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.

blocks.en: 1. Introduction
blocks.zh: 一、导 言 导言

blocks.en:
Byte-level models avoid a fixed tokenizer by working on raw bytes and
recover efficiency by grouping bytes into variable-length patches [ Pagnoni et al., 2025 , Slagle, 2024 , Hwang et al., 2026 ] . In BLT [ Pagnoni et al., 2025 ] , a small byte-level language model estimates the
entropy of each next byte, a patch starts where that entropy crosses a
threshold, and the large global transformer runs once per patch. The
guiding principle, shared by later work, is that compute should go where
prediction is hard: Scratchpad Patching triggers extra global steps by
next-byte entropy [ Zheng et al., 2026 ] , and SOMBRERO trains
learned chunkers to place boundaries on high-surprisal bytes [ Neitemeier et al., 2026 ] .

blocks.en:
Earlier work identified a blind spot in this principle [ Vera Zúñiga, 2026 ] . At a computed result, such as the number after 16 - 3 - 4 = , the next byte is a digit whose value
requires computation over context the local model cannot see, yet the
byte does not look unusually surprising to the small patcher. Under
tight patch budgets, an entropy threshold spends patches on
hard-to-predict prose and skips these positions, and accuracy on them
collapses. That work proposed boundary dependence , a table of how
much the model’s own loss rises when a patch start is removed, as a
label-free fix.

blocks.en:
Here we take a different, cheaper route, motivated by compression. An
LZ77 compressor [ Ziv and Lempel, 1977 ] encodes text as copies of
earlier substrings plus new literals: copies are cheap, and new literals
are where information enters. We ask whether patch boundaries belong
where the compressor would stop copying. Novelty patching starts
a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the last 128
bytes, predicted from the previous two bytes by a lookup table fitted on
raw text in seconds. It needs no labels, no reference model and no
losses, and at inference it costs a table lookup.

信息输入的地方。 我们问补丁边界是否属于

blocks.zh: 2. 国家 相关工作

blocks.en:
Patching rules. BLT [ Pagnoni et al., 2025 ] uses a global
entropy threshold (and an approximate monotonic variant); entropy spikes
as boundaries go back to dynamic pooling [ Nawrot et al., 2023 ] .
SpaceByte [ Slagle, 2024 ] patches at word boundaries; H-Net [ Hwang et al., 2026 ] , AU-Net [ Videau et al., 2025 ] , MrT5 [ Kallini et al., 2024 ] and ByteSpan [ Goriely et al., 2025 ] learn
or derive boundaries in other ways. Scratchpad Patching [ Zheng et al., 2026 ] adds entropy-triggered global steps inside
fixed patches, Fast BLT [ Kallini et al., 2026 ] speeds up decoding,
and EntropyMoE [ Liu et al., 2026 ] routes patches to experts by
entropy. Haltiuk [ Haltiuk, 2026 ] argues that the
boundary distribution can be changed nearly independently of language

blocks.en:
Boundaries and surprisal. SOMBRERO [ Neitemeier et al., 2026 ] defines boundary enrichment , the
mean surprisal at chunk starts relative to all bytes, and trains a
hierarchical byte model to raise it; it reports bits per byte (including
math and code) and log-likelihood downstream tasks at 1B scale, but not
accuracy on computed values. ByteFlow [ Deng et al., 2026 ] selects
boundaries by the marginal coding-rate gain of the encoder’s latent
states, a learned, latent notion of new information, and reports that it
beats an entropy criterion inside its architecture on bits per byte and
commonsense tasks. Our results are consistent with ByteFlow’s direction
and quantify it on answer accuracy.

two sides of the same coin [ Delétang et al., 2024 ] .

inference to merge recurring tokens into hypertokens, which shortens
sequences; we use the LZ notion of reuse for a different purpose,
deciding where a model spends global compute.

blocks.en: 3. Method and setup
blocks.zh: 3个 方法和设置

blocks.en:
Novelty. For a byte stream b b , let m t m_{t} be the length of
the longest prefix of b t : b_{t:} that also starts within the previous
128 bytes (capped at 16). Novelty is − m t -m_{t} : high when the upcoming
bytes do not repeat recent context. Novelty depends on future bytes, so
it cannot be used directly; we predict it causally. The novelty table
averages − m t -m_{t} over each preceding two-byte context ( b t − 2 , b t − 1 ) (b_{t-2},b_{t-1}) in a 4 MB sample of training text (falling back
to one byte, then the global mean, for contexts seen fewer than 20
times). A patch starts at t t when the table value exceeds a threshold
set on training text for a target rate. Fitting takes seconds on a CPU;
applying it is a lookup per byte. We fit two tables: nov , on
GSM8K and MATH training solutions (as in the earlier dependence table),
and novc , on 4 MB sampled from the raw pretraining corpus, with
no math-specific selection.

blocks.en:
Models and data. BLT-style models (cross-attention pooling,
windowed local decoder, 128-byte context) at three sizes: 1M (width 128,
4 global layers, 131M training bytes), 12M (320, 8 layers, 0.5B bytes)
and 50M (576, 12 layers, 1.5B bytes), all trained from scratch on the
same 1.9 GB corpus (OpenWebMath [ Paster et al., 2024 ] shards
plus GSM8K [ Cobbe et al., 2021 ] and MATH [ Hendrycks et al., 2021 ] training solutions repeated to 10% of bytes; SHA-256 pinned; documents
overlapping the evaluation set removed). Each rule’s threshold targets
10% of training bytes (13% for novc), which gives 10.9–12.1% of
evaluation bytes (entropy 11.2%, dependence 10.9%, novelty 11.9%,
corpus-fitted novelty 11.4%). At 50M all runs use gradient clipping at
norm 1.0, which we checked to be neutral for the baselines (entropy
without clipping: final answers 59.0% vs 59.9% with it).

blocks.en:
Table 1 shows the main result. At 1M every rule is near the floor on
computed results (3–5%), and only the hand-written rule lifts final
answers (one dependence seed diverged at 1M, hence its bits per byte).
At 12M novelty raises final answers by 25 points over entropy (71.5% vs
46.6%; every seed separates) and over the dependence table (56.7%),
and computed results from 5.8% to 10.1%. At 50M the gap is large on
both targets: computed results 57.5% vs 20.7% (entropy) and 35.1%
(dependence), final answers 89.5% vs 59.9% and 78.2%. Entropy’s
computed accuracy varies widely across seeds (12.1, 27.5 and 22.6%),
but its best seed is far below novelty’s worst (56.3%). The effect
grows with model size (Figure 1): no difference at 1M, a 25-point
final-answer gain at 12M, and 30 points on final answers and 37 on
computed results at 50M.

Computed results are not surprising to the patcher. We compute

patching, on the math evaluation set at the exact thresholds of the 50M
runs (Table 4). Entropy has the highest enrichment ( B = 1.61 B=1.61 , Z = 215 Z=215 against a rate-matched circular-shift null) and starts a

Novelty finds segment starts in math, not in code. In math, the
novelty table’s strongest contexts are a word followed by ? ,
the end of a question where a solution begins, and it starts a patch at

code it starts a patch at none of the statement starts and none of the

boundaries fall inside identifiers (50% by chance), mostly in hex and
escape literals: content that is genuinely unrepeated but carries no
structure. The limitation is in the target, not only in the two-byte
predictor: even the true novelty target covers only 18% of statement
starts in code, and a 128-byte network that predicts the target better
(rank correlation 0.52 vs 0.39) covers 9%.

blocks.en: 8. Limitations
blocks.zh: 8. 限制

blocks.en:
Scale. Our models are at most 50M parameters trained from
scratch, plus inference-only layouts on BLT-1B. The trend from 1M to 50M
favours novelty, but the methods we compare against run at 1B and above,
where a stronger patcher might find computed results more surprising. A
preregistered scale-up (150M models from scratch, and full fine-tuning
of BLT-1B with frozen patchers) is designed but not yet run.

blocks.en: 9. Conclusion
blocks.zh: 9. 国家 结论

blocks.en:
Where should a byte-level model spend its global compute? The prevailing
answer, where the next byte is hard to predict, misses positions whose
value must be computed but whose surprisal is ordinary. A compression
view gives a different answer: where the text stops repeating.
Implemented as a two-byte lookup table fitted in seconds, it raises
computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy
from 60% to 90% in 50M-parameter models on math, with an effect that
grows with scale, and it costs nothing at inference. Its reach is
limited to text where new content begins at segment starts near the
computation; learned chunkers find such structure more generally. The
practical message for patcher design is to stop treating surprisal as
the target: on math, the rules that concentrate boundaries most on
surprising bytes compute worst.
